e.meaning: from Atharvan, a sage of the Vedas
e.etymology: From Sanskrit Atharvan, the name of a legendary Vedic sage and fire priest. The Atharva Veda, one of the four Vedas, is named for him.
A 20th-century American coinage from Jay plus Lee, in the same family as Kaylee and Jaylynn.
From Arabic layth, a literary word for lion. A separate Scottish surname Laith is tied to the place name Leith.
The Italian form of Charles, from Latin Carolus, from a Germanic word for a free man. Carlo Acutis, an Italian teenager who died in 2006, was canonized in 2025 as the first millennial saint.
A Latinate form of Adele, the short form of Germanic names beginning with adal (noble). Adela of Normandy, a daughter of William the Conqueror, carried it into medieval England.

e.meaning: Greek form of Helen, often read as torch or shining light
e.etymology: The modern Greek form of Helen, from ancient Greek Helene, the name of Helen of Troy. Its root is uncertain; it has long been linked to Greek words for a torch and for the light of the sun.

e.meaning: from Meurig, the Welsh form of Maurice
e.etymology: From a surname that anglicizes the Welsh name Meurig, the Welsh form of Maurice, from Latin Mauricius (Moorish, dark). It rose as a first name in the 2010s.

e.meaning: joyful celebration; a biblical year of release
e.etymology: The English word for a season of celebration, from Hebrew yovel (ram's horn), the trumpet that announced the biblical Jubilee year, when debts were forgiven and slaves went free.

assoc.t: Jubilee, the X-Men mutant who throws fireworks
Jubilee, YouTube channel behind Middle Ground and Surrounded

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Cole, an English surname from the Old English byname Cola (coal-dark, swarthy) that also served as a medieval short form of Nicholas. Kole is separately an anglicized form of the German surname Kohl.
The Hebrew original of Solomon, from shalom (peace), the name of the biblical king famed for his wisdom. In the US it is used almost entirely in Orthodox Jewish families.
A modern spelling, probably of Mia, which began as a Scandinavian and German pet form of Maria. Some families say it MY-uh, like Maya or the end of Jeremiah.
The Spanish and Italian spelling of Daphne, Greek for laurel. In myth the nymph Daphne was turned into a laurel tree to escape the god Apollo.
namesakes: Dafne Keen (actress, Logan and His Dark Materials)

e.etymology: A respelling of Addison, an English surname meaning son of Addie, a medieval pet form of Adam. Addison took off as a girls' name in the 2000s.
First a short form of Honora and Honoria, from Latin honor, and later taken up by the Puritans as a virtue name. Honour is the British spelling.
namesakes: Honor Blackman (actress who played Pussy Galore in Goldfinger)

e.etymology: A recent American name of unsettled origin. It shares its sound with Isaiah and Azariah, and the same spelling turns up as a Japanese clan name and, as Azzai, in the name of the Talmudic sage Simeon ben Azzai.

e.meaning: short for Terence or Theresa; as a surname, ruler of the people
e.etymology: A short form of Terence, from the Roman family name Terentius, and of Theresa. It is also a surname from the medieval name Thierry, the French form of Theodoric (ruler of the people).
namesakes: Terry Bradshaw (Hall of Fame quarterback and broadcaster)
Terry Gross (host of NPR's Fresh Air)

assoc.t: terry cloth, the looped towel fabric
Terry's Chocolate Orange, the holiday candy

e.etymology: From Sanskrit Mira, the name of Meera Bai, a 16th-century Rajput princess and poet-saint famous for her songs of devotion to Krishna.
A recent coinage made popular by Dalary Hernandez, younger daughter of singer Larry Hernandez, on the Spanish-language reality show Larrymania. Her sister's name, Daleyza, rose the same way.
The French form of Dominic, from Late Latin Dominicus (of the Lord), used in France for both men and women.
namesakes: Dominique Wilkins (Hall of Fame NBA forward)

e.etymology: From the ancient Greek name Dion, a short form of names beginning with Dio- (of Zeus). It was also a medieval English and French pet form of Dionysius, the source of Dennis.
namesakes: Dion DiMucci (singer of Runaround Sue and The Wanderer)

e.etymology: The Spanish word for April, from the Latin month name Aprilis, which may go back to a name for the goddess Aphrodite.
The Spanish and Portuguese word for blue, which goes back through Arabic to the Persian word for lapis lazuli, the same source as English azure.
A modern American spelling in the Adeline and Adalyn family, written as if it were Addie plus Lynn. Adeline is a French pet form of Adele, from Germanic adal (noble).
A spelling of Hayley, an English surname from a place name, Old English heg (hay) plus leah (clearing). The fame of child actress Hayley Mills in the 1960s turned it into a girls' name.

From an English surname and place name, Old English for Hroda's island, where Hroda is a short name built on a word for fame. The naval victories of Admiral George Rodney in the 18th century made it a first name.
namesakes: Rodney King (whose 1991 beating by Los Angeles police led to the 1992 riots)

e.etymology: From Greek Demetrios, belonging to Demeter, the goddess of grain and the harvest. Saint Demetrius made it a favorite in the Orthodox world, and this spelling reached English through French and Russian.
namesakes: Dimitri (the con man hero of the animated film Anastasia)

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Grayson, an English surname meaning son of the grieve, a northern word for a steward or bailiff. Today it is often heard simply as a longer form of Gray.
A modern American coinage with no known source, close in sound to Kamari, Amora and Zamora.
The name of a heroine of the Welsh Mabinogi, probably from the Old Celtic title Rigantona (great queen). It spread through the English-speaking world after Fleetwood Mac's 1975 song Rhiannon.
From an English surname and place name, Old English ansetl (hermitage) plus leah (woodland clearing). As a girls' name it is a favorite in the American South.

e.meaning: from mazzikin, harmful spirits in Jewish folklore
e.etymology: Created by Neil Gaiman for a demon in The Sandman comics, from mazzikin, a Hebrew and Aramaic word for harmful spirits. Parents know it from Maze, the demon bartender and bounty hunter of the TV series Lucifer.

assoc.t: Mazikeen (Maze), the demon in the TV series Lucifer

e.note: The name comes from a word for demons, and the character who made it known is a demon from Hell.

e.etymology: From a surname with two sources: English place names such as Willey (willow clearing), and the Scottish Wylie, a pet form of William. It was a fairly common American first name in the 19th century.
namesakes: Wiley Post (aviator who made the first solo flight around the world)

assoc.t: Wile E. Coyote of Looney Tunes (sounds the same)
Wiley, publisher of textbooks and the For Dummies books

e.note: Sounds the same as wily, meaning cunning, and as Wile E. Coyote.
